title: Maximum Sum of Two Non-Overlapping Subarrays
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair of window positions with prefix sums versus a single linear sweep per ordering that carries a running best window sum.

content.title: Maximum Sum of Two Non-Overlapping Subarrays

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and two integers firstLen and secondLen, return the maximum sum obtainable by picking two non-overlapping (but not necessarily adjacent) contiguous subarrays, one of length exactly firstLen and one of length exactly secondLen, in either left-to-right order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, firstLen (L), secondLen (M)"],["Output","The maximum combined sum of one length-L window and one length-M window that do not overlap"],["Goal","Consider both possible left-to-right orders of the two windows, without checking every pair of positions one at a time"],["Constraints","1 <= L, M; L + M <= nums.length <= 1000; 0 <= nums[i] <= 1000"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Two FIXED-length windows must be chosen at once","A fixed-size sliding window for each length, combined together"],["The windows cannot overlap, but either can come first","Two separate left-to-right sweeps, one per ordering, taking the better result"],["Only the best window seen so far to one side matters at each point","A running maximum carried alongside a sliding prefix sum, the same shape as Kadane's running best"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given nums, firstLen, and secondLen, choose a contiguous block of exactly firstLen elements and a separate contiguous block of exactly secondLen elements, with no shared index between them, so that their combined sum is as large as possible.

blocks.title: Analogy: Picking Two Best Non-Overlapping Vacation Weeks
blocks.text: Imagine a year of daily earnings, and needing to pick one L-day vacation and one separate M-day vacation, never on overlapping days, to maximize total earnings collected. The two vacations can happen in either order during the year.

blocks.caption: Either window can appear first, both orders must be checked

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [0, 6, 5, 2, 2, 5, 1, 9, 4], firstLen = 1, secondLen = 2
The best choice is the length-1 window [9] and the length-2 window [6,5] (or an equally good pairing), giving a combined sum of 20.
Example: nums = [3, 8, 1, 3, 2, 1, 8, 9, 0], firstLen = 3, secondLen = 2
Picking the length-3 window [3,8,1] and the length-2 window [8,9] gives the combined sum 29.
Edge case: the two lengths are equal
When firstLen equals secondLen, the two windows are interchangeable, only their non-overlapping combined sum matters, not which one is labeled "first."
5. How Should We Think?
Before searching every pair of positions, notice that once the two windows are laid out left to right, one of them strictly precedes the other, there are only two possible orderings to consider.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed order, say the L window before the M window, sliding the M window from left to right, the best possible L window is always somewhere in the untouched prefix strictly to its left.

Observation 2: That best-L-window-so-far only ever grows or stays the same as the M window slides further right, so it can be tracked with a single running maximum, updated once per step.

Observation 3: Prefix sums turn any window's sum into a single subtraction, so both the running best L window and the current M window can be evaluated in O(1) per position.

Observation 4: The other order, M window before L window, is symmetric, simply swap the roles and repeat the same sweep.
This leads directly to two linear sweeps, one per ordering, each maintaining a running best window sum on one side and combining it with the current window on the other side.
6. Brute Force Solution
Try every valid pair of start positions for the two windows, using prefix sums to get each window's sum in O(1), and keep the best non-overlapping combined sum found.
Step by step algorithm

items: Build a prefix sum array so any window's sum is one subtraction away.
For every start position i of the length-L window, and every start position j of the length-M window, check whether the two windows overlap.
If they do not overlap, compute their combined sum and update the running best.
Return the best combined sum found across every valid pair.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every pair of window positions directly

codes.python:
def max_sum_two_no_overlap(nums, L, M):
    n = len(nums)
    prefix = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]

    best = 0
    for i in range(n - L + 1):                     # every start of the L window
        for j in range(n - M + 1):                  # every start of the M window
            if i + L <= j or j + M <= i:             # only accept non-overlapping pairs
                total = (prefix[i + L] - prefix[i]) + (prefix[j + M] - prefix[j])
                best = max(best, total)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_sum_two_no_overlap([0, 6, 5, 2, 2, 5, 1, 9, 4], 1, 2))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Prefix sums are built once up front, so every individual window sum inside the double loop costs O(1) instead of re-adding L or M elements.
The overlap check, i + L <= j or j + M <= i, is the direct condition for two intervals to be disjoint, one window ending at or before the other begins.
Every valid non-overlapping pair is checked independently, with no memory carried between iterations.

Dry run for a small array

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pair checked","Overlap?","Result"],"rows":[["L window at 0, M window at 1","Overlaps if L > 1","Skipped when the windows share an index"],["L window at 0, M window at L","No overlap","Combined sum computed and compared to the running best"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair of start positions for the two windows.
Space: O(n) for the prefix sum array.

Limitation: most of the n squared pairs are wasted work, once the windows are considered in a fixed left-to-right order, the best window on one side only needs to be tracked once while sweeping, not recomputed against every possible position on the other side.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair is wasteful: for a fixed ordering, say L before M, the best L window for a given M window position is simply the best L window seen anywhere strictly before it, and that best-so-far never needs to be recomputed from every earlier position again.

What changes as the M window slides right: the set of valid L window positions only grows, so the best L window seen so far can only increase or stay the same.

What about the other ordering: M before L is exactly symmetric, sliding an L window right while tracking the best M window seen so far to its left.

The core idea: run one linear sweep per ordering, carrying a running best window sum on one side, and combining it with the current window sum on the other side at every step.

For the ordering "L window, then M window", slide the M window across the array, and before combining, update a running maximum of every L window that fits entirely before the M window's current position. Repeat the same sweep with the roles swapped for "M window, then L window", and return the better of the two results.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for nums = [0, 6, 5, 2, 2, 5, 1, 9, 4], firstLen = 1, secondLen = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["M window ends at index","Best L window strictly before it","Combined candidate"],"rows":[["3 (M = [6,5])","Best L window in [0]: value 0","0 + 11 = 11"],["8 (M = [1,9])","Best L window in [0..5]: value 6","6 + 10 = 16"],["9 (M = [9,4])","Best L window in [0..6]: value 6","6 + 13 = 19 (a later step reaches the true best, 20)"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one running best carried alongside a sliding window, per ordering

codes.python:
def max_sum_two_no_overlap(nums, L, M):
    n = len(nums)
    prefix = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]

    def best_order(first, second):                  # 'first' window comes before 'second' window
        ans, max_first = 0, 0
        for i in range(first + second, n + 1):
            max_first = max(max_first, prefix[i - second] - prefix[i - second - first])
            ans = max(ans, max_first + prefix[i] - prefix[i - second])
        return ans

    return max(best_order(L, M), best_order(M, L))  # try both left-to-right orderings


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_sum_two_no_overlap([0, 6, 5, 2, 2, 5, 1, 9, 4], 1, 2))

blocks.text: Why This Works

At every position i where the second window ends, every first window that fits entirely before it is a valid, non-overlapping candidate, and max_first already holds the best sum among all of them, since it only grows as i advances. Combining that running best with the current second window's sum, at every single position, guarantees the true best pairing for that ordering is found; running the same sweep with the two lengths swapped covers the other ordering, and the true answer is the better of the two.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear sweeps over the array, one per ordering.
Space: O(n) for the prefix sum array.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem combines two ideas seen elsewhere on this sheet: prefix sums for O(1) window sums, and a running maximum carried across a single sweep, the same shape as Kadane's Algorithm. The only extra twist is that the two windows can appear in either order, so the sweep must be run once per ordering.
Common Mistakes

items: Only checking one ordering of the two windows and missing the case where the better arrangement has the other window on the left.
Recomputing every window sum from scratch inside the sweep instead of using prefix sums.
Allowing the two windows to overlap by getting the boundary condition wrong when sliding the second window.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["firstLen equals secondLen","The two windows are interchangeable; only the non-overlapping combined sum matters."],["firstLen + secondLen equals nums.length","The two windows must exactly tile the entire array, with no slack on either side."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Mentioning upfront that the two windows can appear in either order, and that this is why two separate sweeps are needed, shows the full problem has been understood before any code is written.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every pair", think: track a running best window sum on one side while sliding the other window across.
If the interviewer says "what if the better answer has the windows in the other order", think: run the same sweep twice, once per ordering, and take the better result.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this extend to three non-overlapping fixed-length windows instead of two?
Can you avoid the O(n) prefix sum array and use O(1) extra space with a pure sliding window sum instead?
How does this relate to the single fixed-size sliding window maximum problems solved elsewhere on this sheet?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Kadane's Algorithm, this problem carries a running best sum across a sweep in the same way, just for a fixed-size window instead of a variable-length one.
Prefix Sum problems in general, where any window sum becomes a single subtraction, is the foundation this sweep is built on.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized running-best sweep runs in O(n) time, both using O(n) space for the prefix sum array.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: two fixed-size sliding windows combined with a running maximum, checked in both possible left-to-right orderings.
Core Idea: while sweeping one window across the array, track the best value of the other window seen so far strictly on one side, instead of checking every pair of positions.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized sweep.
Space: O(n) for the prefix sum array in both versions.
Most Important Observation: once an ordering of the two windows is fixed, the best window on one side only needs to be tracked once while sweeping, never recomputed against every earlier position.
Interview Difficulty: the prefix sum and running max ideas are individually simple; remembering to check both orderings is the detail that is easiest to miss.
One line memory trick: a running best window, carried alongside a sliding window, checked both ways round.
